analysis.one_liner: Orders the Labor Department to write a workplace ergonomics rule to prevent repetitive-stress injuries.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill requiring the Labor Department to write a new workplace ergonomics rule never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the Labor Department to issue a workplace ergonomics standard within two years — rules that make employers change jobs and workstations that cause back injuries, carpal tunnel syndrome, and other repetitive-stress injuries. The bill came just weeks after Congress repealed the first-ever OSHA ergonomics rule issued at the end of the Clinton administration, and it was written more narrowly: it covered only work-related conditions, required clear compliance obligations for employers, and left state workers' compensation systems untouched. It never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate labor committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in jobs with heavy lifting, repetitive motion, or awkward postures — meatpacking, manufacturing, warehouse, grocery, and nursing home work, among others. The bill's own findings say about a million workers a year lose time from work to these injuries, costing the economy $45–54 billion annually. A standard would force employers to fix the hazardous jobs before workers get hurt, cutting injuries, lost wages, and lost work time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers in repetitive-motion and lifting jobs

how_it_helps.text: The bill found that about 1,000,000 workers each year lose time from work because of work-related musculoskeletal disorders, and that the economic burden runs between $45 billion and $54 billion a year.

It directed the Secretary of Labor to issue a final rule within two years that addresses work-related musculoskeletal disorders and workplace ergonomic hazards, to take effect within 90 days of being issued.
It required the Labor Department to prepare training materials and an outreach program so employers and workers know how to comply.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would have to identify hazardous jobs, redesign workstations and processes, and train workers. The bill tried to limit the cost by covering only work-related conditions and spelling out employer obligations in clear terms, but a mandatory standard would still mean real compliance spending across labor-intensive industries.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers facing redesign and training costs

drawbacks.text: The bill acknowledges that any standard must take into account the cost and feasibility of compliance; employers, especially small businesses in labor-intensive industries, would bear the cost of redesigning workstations, training workers, and changing processes.

The bill excludes musculoskeletal disorders that occur outside the workplace or that are merely aggravated by work, and it bars the new rule from expanding state workers' compensation laws, so some injured workers with mixed causes would fall outside the standard's protections.

Work-related musculoskeletal disorders are often hard to attribute to the job, a good-faith concern of opponents; a mandatory standard could still require employers to act in cases where the work connection is genuinely disputed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On the merits, the bill was a modest, carefully limited mandate: a federal standard to prevent roughly a million lost-work-time injuries a year, written to exclude non-work-related conditions and to leave state workers' compensation untouched. The cost falls on employers, who would need to evaluate jobs and fix hazardous ones, and honest supporters would concede that compliance costs fall hardest on small businesses and that attributing a given back injury to work can be genuinely hard. But the bill was drafted specifically to answer the cost and causation objections raised against the earlier 2000 rule, and its death meant the $45–54 billion annual toll of these injuries continued to land on injured workers, their families, and public compensation systems with no federal prevention standard in place. The main cost of a bad outcome here was borne by the people the bill was written for.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 22, 2001, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
That referral was the last action ever recorded; the committee held no markup and the Senate never voted on it, and it expired when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

The bill cited a January 2001 National Academy of Sciences report finding that work-related musculoskeletal disorders are an important and costly national health problem, with about a million workers losing work time each year and an economic burden of $45–54 billion annually.
It would have overridden normal rulemaking delays by requiring the Secretary of Labor to issue a final ergonomics rule within two years, taking effect within 90 days of issuance.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced the cost of a mandatory ergonomics standard are better off, since the bill died without a vote. Workers with repetitive-stress injuries got no new federal protection; Congress had already repealed the first OSHA ergonomics rule in March 2001, and none replaced it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided a mandatory ergonomics standard

for.name: Sen. John Breaux
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing the Labor Secretary to issue a new ergonomics rule, with findings on the cost of musculoskeletal disorders.

for.name: 8 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Lincoln, Landrieu, Cleland, Miller, Johnson, and three others).

for.name: 3 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Specter, Stevens, and Nelson of Nebraska).

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business coalitions
against.what_they_did: Fought federal ergonomics regulation; the successful campaign to repeal the 2000 OSHA ergonomics rule concluded just weeks before this bill was introduced, and no mandatory ergonomics standard advanced during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was evenly bipartisan — one Democratic sponsor, 8 Democratic and 3 Republican cosponsors — and there is no recorded floor opposition, but the bill never reached a vote in the Republican- or Democrat-led committee that received it.

industries.industry: Employers in labor-intensive industries (meatpacking, manufacturing, warehouses, nursing homes, grocery and retail)
industries.note: The bill would have forced a mandatory federal standard requiring these employers to act on ergonomic hazards, with training and outreach before it took effect. They had just escaped exactly this kind of rule when Congress repealed the 2000 OSHA ergonomics standard weeks earlier, and this bill died without a vote.

industries.industry: State workers' compensation systems and their insurers
industries.note: The bill expressly prohibited the new rule from expanding the application of state workers' compensation laws, keeping employer liability in that system unchanged. Workers with mixed work and non-work causes would have stayed outside comp coverage.
